chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Coleman Hawkins and the Selmer advertisements
summary: Selmer's pictures of Hawkins with a gold Selmer drove McRae and many tenor players to switch; Hawkins visited the Savoy.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Some of the top soloists and even some who weren't some top soloists, (inaudible) used to be featured in ads and advertising in some of the trade papers and trade magazines for, you know, so and so plays Conn horns, Martin (inaudible) horns --
Well I think I --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
-- Selmer horns.
Well this is what brought the Selmer horn to my attention.
Selmer gave Coleman Hawkins a horn, a gold horn, he told me. And they used his picture -- Coleman Hawkins playing the Selmer.
And they had it in the DownBeat, they had it in the little French papers. That time we used to go to 42nd Street and get all the French magazines -- all the magazines come out of --
Jazz (inaudible). Hot.
Jazz (inaudible) and all that stuff. And they Selmer and -- playing all these horns, you know, different -- Selmer -- that was it.
Whatever Coleman Hawkins played, that's it. He's the daddy. Coleman was the boss, (inaudible) of the tenor.
No greater tenor player ever lived than Coleman Hawkins. Today you ain't gonna find one.
You can play some of Coleman Hawkins' records right now, and you find me some tenor player pedd'n (inaudible) what Coleman is playing
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
on (inaudible). They can play. If you'd just break it down and listen to what he's playing, listening to what he's trying to play, that's a man that knew that instrument backwards. Good arranger too.

So Coleman Hawkins was the boss. He gave us three or four different styles of things. When they brought up (Inaudible) that incident about Chu Berry and what he was supposed to do, he never scratched the surface when it come down to playing (inaudible) with Coleman.
Good tenor player. Coleman was considered the boss. All these guys (inaudible). (Inaudible). Coleman could play brass like anybody else.
You got a lot of records where he's playing (inaudible) clean, you know. When Coleman came out with the Selmer, everybody jumped to the Selmer. So that's why I jumped.

Coleman come up to the Savoy -- he say, "I see you playing what I got." I say, "Yeah." When he came back from Europe (Inaudible) come up the Savoy. He wanted (Inaudible) come up and see you. "At least you're

not playing me, you're playing yourself. Playing your own ideas."
